review:
Long Gone Days wonderful game with beautiful art and a captivating story.

To be honest, I don't think the story is going to surprise anyone, but it's a story excellently told and thoroughly enjoyable nonetheless. We follow Rourke, a young man bred from birth to be a sniper for a secret military group. Rourke learns about the reality of the outside world and the truth of his upbringing, and goes on a journey to essentially find peace. Unfortunately, conflict is unavoidable, but I think a key part of the story is that some things are truly worth fighting for, and anyone is capable of fighting for those things.

I loved the story and the characters, and the game had me hooked from start to finish. Rourke is a more interesting protagonist than he looks, and the game executes the "stranger in a strange land" aspect of him and his buddy Adair excellently. Every character is endearing (and their designs are gorgeous), and I loved how they were all able to find commonality in such hard situations. The fact that characters come from different countries and are unable to understand one another is a neat hurdle to overcome. Atiye is probably my favorite character, but I won't deny that part of that is probably because she's so pretty- though she is also funny and very charming.

Combat looks really interesting, but I found it to be a bit too easy. You don't have to face every enemy on the maps, and there's no experience or levels. As long as you keep equipment updated, characters will learn new skills as the story progresses, so there's a pretty steady curve of difficulty. That being said, I think the curve flattens out pretty early; only the first boss was really intimidating. During boss fights, there will be some dialogue which connects to the alternate story paths possible. I think that really adds to the vibe of the game and takes the presentation up to a really stellar level.

Overall I think it's a wonderful game with a relatively concise story. My only real gripe is that the controls on keyboard are a little weird, but you don't have to be very dexterous to play this game. I highly recommend this as a very charming and captivating RPG!
Unfortunately a pretty toothless and ineffective story wrapped in repetitive, barebones gameplay. Pretty art, I guess?

This game is a total rugpull. If you thought you were going to play an exciting RPG about soldiers on the modern battlefield, guess again… it’s basically an angry leftist simulator with all the basic talking points you see in every “anti war” story. In short:
Military bad
War bad
Authority bad
Hierarchy bad
Questioning authority good
Rebellion ALWAYS good
Normal family bad
Found family good
Imagine playing Call of Duty, or Metal Gear Solid, basically any military themed game, but after they set the scene and you have all this cool military type stuff going on, it quickly switches to a Bong Rip simulator where you have to waste time talking to disgruntled leftists who are living out their fantasy of being chased down by the military? It’s crazy how RPG players will eat this slop up and imagine it’s deep and meaningful. As if ignoring the importance of conflict in human history, even its importance to the human soul, is somehow less important than being an angry anti-authoritarian goofball with no direction in life. Thanks but no thanks.
What are the chances that this is another fake “indie” game getting tons of money from NGOs and government sources? Do I even need to take the time to find out? Or is it a safe assumption at this point?

Long Gone Days is a classic-style 2D RPG with turn-based battles. In terms of gameplay and mechanics it's very familiar and reminiscent of the 2D RPGs we're used to. 

However, it's not just another medieval fantasy story that we've seen many times already. The story here takes place in a modern day world (possibly very near future). We start as part of a top secret special force of young soldiers who have been trained since childhood and who undertake important missions around the globe.

Although the story is for the most part rather predictable, and plot twists and revelations won't particularly catch you off-guard, I think the main appeal here is more in the characters, their interactions with each other and the world, as well as their overall journey and how they try to cope with reality of the unfolding events.

Another interesting aspect of story execution is what we don't normally see in such stories - the language barriers. Most of the game's events occur in Kaliningrad, Germany and Poland. So, our starting characters speaking primarily in English, struggle to understand the NPCs who ask for help or merely comment their thoughts out loud. And even if you may understand the NPCs who speak Russian, German or Polish, the main characters do not, and so they are unable to help the NPCs, until certain party members join the team who understand each of those languages and can help us progress the quests. It's a very interesting take on story-telling that often gets overlooked in majority of other story-driven games that span multiple countries or continents.

In each of the new locations we visit, we get given plenty of sidequests that we can do in addition to the main story. Most of those are merely ways to help NPCs and increase our morale. Now I didn't see the morale having any combat-related impact, but I am pretty sure the game promises it affects story events. It might be necessary to have multiple playthroughs of the game to really see these story changes though. The only one I am aware of is that it's very hard to get a good ending to the story, because certain conditions need to be met to achieve it, which was a bit disappointing, because the default ending you get doesn't feel like a satisfying conclusion to this long journey our characters have gone through.

The turn-based combat to me felt so-so. One aspect I appreciated was the chance to choose which enemy body part we can shoot at. Unfortunately this concept doesn't change much beyond the initial introduction, as all human enemies only have 3 points really: head, body and arm, with the head being the area you want to go for 90% of the time in order to maximise the damage (at a slightly higher chance to miss). There are a few machine enemies that have other types of parts we can aim for, but it's usually just a trade-off: hit a part with high def and low chance to miss, or try to go for a low def part with a higher chance to miss. Most times, the low def part is the better option. Unfortunately, the game never tells us what the % chance to miss is, which brings me to a wider critique of battles...

This critique is that we get very little numerical information about everything in battles - how high is the evasion rate, how high is an Atk buff worth or an Atk debuff, how many turns do status effects last, how much damage does bleed status do (and whether it's a flat amount or percentage amount), and so on. In fact much of this information isn't even shown on the battle HUD. You get told when you get a buff or a debuff, but there's no indication on characters if they have a buff/debuff active currently. You only see this with status effects, shown as icons.

In addition to lack of info on the battle screen, the battle speed is also very slow (I can't remember if there was an option to speed it up, but the default speed is slow). The main issue really is when buffs/debuffs are applied. If they're applied to a whole party, you'll have to wait for an individual message to show up about each of your party member, which takes a big chunk of time.

Generally, the battles left a lot to be desired, especially the boss fights, which mostly felt like regular enemies but with a 10x more HP, so just a much longer regular battle. To me the main challenge was in trying to deal as much damage as possible to make their HP bar deplete faster, rather than worrying about my people getting killed. Even with the special skills that our characters use, the damage was often not enough.

In the presentation area the game shines. It has a very beautiful and colourful art style, with both characters and environments being drawn beautifully. And the special cutscenes are even better, which felt like animated movies produced by a professional studio. Only minor gripe I'd say is with the item menu. It gets filled up with items very quickly, and navigating through it to find what you need can be a bit of a chore, especially because all the icons are the same colour.

Despite a so-so execution to the turn-based battles, which make up the major aspect of the gameplay, the game has a decent story and characters that's worth experiencing, and a high quality visual presentation. So if you're mainly looking for a game with good turn-based battles, this one will disappoint you, but if you want to go through a nice JRPG story that's unique and interesting, then I'd recommend getting it on a discount.

I had wanted to play this game for some time, and I finally did! And I've finished the game! 

First of all, I really enjoy the game. I think it's fun! I like the concept of the game. The art is great, and the pixel environment is very cool. The music is also nice. The characters are vibrant and interesting. The story has its moments, but overall I think it's good (at least, I have fun!). While the theme is quite heavy, it is conveyed in a more hopeful tone. Rourke and Adair were so lucky that almost everyone they met on the surface was nice. Not knowing any of those languages kinda adds to the experience. I felt relieved when I met the interpreters of each country. Surprisingly, the last boss is easy.

However, there are also some things that I think can be better. While the story is enjoyable, I wish it were a bit longer to expand more about the characters and about the Core. Sometimes the changes are just too sudden, like Rourke, who was said to be indoctrinated, managed to break free quite fast. For the gameplay, I found some minor bugs, but they won't hinder the progression, so I think it's fine. Other than that, the battle can be frustrating at times. It's a bit slow. The enemies evade a lot and paralyze almost never hit. 

Despite what I just listed, I think the game is fun, and I recommend it to people who like RPGs with military and conspiracy stories, but don't want it to have too many complicated drama and conflicts, because life already has a lot of them.

Fui totalmente pega de surpresa por Long Gone Days. É o tipo de jogo que, para mim, se compara a um ótimo filme: a forma como a narrativa se desenrola é simplesmente cativante. A história me envolveu completamente, com seus momentos de tensão, ação intensa e informações secretas (e, quem sabe, até um romance em potencial 🥰).

Ainda não concluí, mas estando nos momentos finais, preciso fazer uma pausa para parabenizar os desenvolvedores pela criatividade. Além do enredo, a jogabilidade também é um ponto forte: as cenas de tiro se intensificam à medida que a história avança, e os inimigos ficam cada vez mais desafiadores.

Long Gone Days entregou tudo o que eu buscava e superou minhas expectativas. É um jogo que terei prazer em revisitar várias vezes, como um filme favorito que nunca enjoa.

Одна из тех немногих игр, где сюжетка о войне не сводится к безликому экшену. Лично для меня, это атмосферная и человечная история, которая оставила небольшой осадок в душе после завершения финальных титров. Музыка тут невероятно шикарная, сильно влияющая на общую атмосферу. Все персонажи которые присоединяются в отряд Рурка, довольно интересные и немного раскрываются, кроме может Ивана, у которого нет какой либо предыстории или развития. Единственный минус кроме Ивана в игре это то, что большинство доп квестов не имеют вариативности. Но в целом, это реально кайфовая игра.

[b]Если вкратце, гг зовут Рурком, он выращенный под землей молодой солдат-снайпер из милитаристской организации «Ядро», который ни разу не видел солнечного света и обычных людей. Всю жизнь его учили исполнять приказы, и вталкивали в голову что всё что они делают - сражаются со злом и приносят мир во всем мире. Но когда его первая же миссия оборачивается вторжением в нейтральную страну [spoiler]и убийством мирных людей и детей[/spoiler], его убеждения и ценности которыми ему [u]промывали[/u] голову в «Ядре» полностью рушатся. И после этого, он начинает искать себя, и уже [u]собственную[/u] цель и ценности в жизни.[/b]

Для начала следует сказать, что моя любовь к этой игре основана её сюжетным тропом - осознание и принятие своих грехов и ошибок прошлого, а всей дальнейшей жизни - на построение эдакой священной миссии - "помогать и ближнему своему, и чужакам чужеродным". Мне не только важен сам этот антивоенный посыл, сколько его значение для литературы, ведь основав произведение на этом тропе, можно затронуть бесчисленные сложные темы и мотивы - философские, религиозные, обще-человеческие, а также - заглянуть в глубины души "греховного" человека, замаравшего руки - и последнее меня всегда интересовало больше прочего, ведь очень уж я люблю внутренний мир человека и то, как в нём могут уживаться столь многогранные и абстрактные вещи. 

И эта игра определённо попала мне в сердце с дальних подступов, хоть и с глупости персонажей, диалогов, ситуаций и общей недо-прописанности мира хотелось выбить facepalm. Уж особенно после арки с Вебером, и то насколько это нереалистично и наивно со стороны разработчиков - с их-то взглядами, - превратить антивоенную повесть в типичную марвеловскую дичь - с какими-то секретными базами, раздутыми агентурными сетями и т.д. 

Хочется упомянуть, что боёвка весьма примитивная, и если на обычных врагах она вполне работает, то вот на боссах разваливается на части, ведь просто-напросто упираешься в их бесконечное хп и по итогу тратишь все ходы на отхилл и мало что можешь сделать. Бои просто бесцельно растягиваются. Зачем, если в этом нет интереса? - Непонятно, и лучше бы этого не было изначально.

В общем, не до конца доволен качеством этой игры (особенно идиотским третьим актом), и рекомендую покупать по скидке в минимум 50%. Но, самих таких произведений очень уж мало. И, на самом деле, эта игра лишь раззадорила меня в этом отношении, так что - вновь отправляюсь на активные поиски чего-то схожего.

Музыка, кстати, очень классная - атмосферная.

The Long Gone Days - не про войну, а про человека внутри войны. Это история снайпера, который решил больше не быть оружием. Здесь нет героев, есть только люди с виной, страхом и попытками сохранить себя в мире приказов и лжи.

Сюжет не хватает звезд с неба, но человечный, с интересными персонажами. Геймплей простой, с пошаговыми боями и механикой морали, но быстро надоедает из-за повторяемости. Языковой барьер и необходимость перевода - интересное новшество, а пиксельная графика и музыка отлично поддерживают мрачную атмосферу.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
Long Gone Days is a game where I mostly tolerated the gameplay in order to experience the story. Despite advertising itself as a modern JRPG, I would say the moment to moment gameplay was subpar compared to titles thirty years prior such as Final Fantasy I. While the story was intriguing enough to keep my playing, the short length made wanting a little more as not all the characters were as arc'd out as I would have liked.

Overall, I would give Long Gone Days a 6/10. Given the length of the game and its bog standard gameplay, I would say the game is worth approximately $10 to me.

[h1]Review[/h1]
Let's quickly talk about gameplay before we get into the game's story. Despite being a JRPG, Long Gone Days has no exp or leveling with the majority of your stats coming from your equipment and a smaller amount from temporary buffs during battle. Abilities are only gained at certain moments in the story. Additionally, HP and MP are not ever recovered except through the usage of items or abilities. When you combine all of this, it results in fairly monotonous battles as you spam basic attacks because you either have no useful abilities or want to conserve your MP for boss battles. 

Items such as grenades do help to compensate for the lack of abilities early on and while the game is generous in giving you more items, because there are no shops or ways to readily acquire more of the same items, you're always unsure if you should be wasting that particular item or not. Perhaps a way to barter items you have an abundance of for items you're lacking would fit thematically.

The one somewhat interesting mechanic of battles is the ability to target enemy body parts. Aiming for their torso will result in less damage but a higher chance of landing a hit while aiming for their head will result in the opposite. You can also aim at their arms for a chance to paralyze enemies and have them skip their turn entirely. However, I quickly learned that the chance of paralyzing an enemy is so low that it's never worthwhile to target their arms and the increased damage of hitting their head greatly outweighs the reduced hit chance. 

Weirdly, one of the things I did enjoy about combat was being able to see each character's facial expressions throughout the battle. Seeing their determined expressions really made me feel for each character and the struggles they were going through.

Now onto the story. I adore how the game handled multiple languages and I especially loved how you couldn't understand certain NPCs until you acquired a party member that was capable of speaking said language. Rather than create characters that were walking stereotypes to reflect their nationality, using linguistics in this manner allowed the characters to shine through with their own, unique personalities.

I enjoyed the themes that Long Gone Days presented and many of them are relevant in our present day. Totalitarian governments, propaganda, and following orders, some of them hit a little too close to home. The characters were also a delight with it being funny at times seeing how Rourke and Adair were experiencing life outside of The Core.

While I am a fan of shorter games, I do think that Long Gone Days suffers a bit from pacing and could have benefitted from being longer. For example, the game begins in medias res, but we reach that particular point in the story again so quickly that it makes me wonder why we didn't just start the story from the very beginning as opposed needing a flashback. Additionally, the twist where Rourke learns the truth of their mission happens honestly surprised me. Not because I didn't see it coming, but because it happened so quick that I was flabbergasted that the reveal was already here. It's almost as if characters are a little bit TOO emotionally mature, overcoming their trauma and making life-changing decisions before I've even had a chance to get fully invested in their arc (if they even have an arc). 

So yeah, while I did enjoy Long Gone Days, I do think it could use some gameplay improvements as well as a few more moments to develop the characters. For example, the various ship and train rides would have been great moments for the party to simply talk to one another and shoot the ♥♥♥♥. Get us invested into the merry little band. 

While we're here, let me just list a few quality of life things I wish Long Gone Days had:
- The ability to see what buffs your party and enemies currently have
- The ability to see hit chances for basic attacks
- The ability to see hit chances for debuffs
- The ability to see exactly how much HP an enemy has
- The ability to sort items by type
- In-game explanation for what each stat does

Let me preface this by saying that I finished the game and enjoyed it, but I can only recommend it if you can buy it on sale because of the rather short playtime.

--------------------
The Good:

The artstyle is amazing. The game uses a mix of pixel art in the overworld, character portraits in combat and dialogue, and 
full-on vibrant/moving art pieces in some important scenes. The love could be felt everywhere in those special scenes, so much so that I sent a couple as screenshots to my friend so we could admire them together. The main cast of characters are mostly just a bunch of everyday people, and the character design shows that by making the characters look rather normal, but in the best way. They felt real, partially because of the art. Standouts in the characters design for me were Beqiri, Coyle and Pascal (mostly because he somehow looks like my friend, who's also named Pascal). The pixel art sprites were very well done and while the environments weren't anything too special, the art depicted was still charming to look at.

The gameplay is (mostly) very fun. I'm a sucker for simple RPGs, and the gameplay fit that bill. Part of why the game only took me around 13 hours to beat is because there's no experience system, no difficulty spikes and no grinding (thank god). The combat is enjoyable and easy to understand. Each party member has a specific role that they can fulfill, with my favourite "combat" character being Ivan. His skills are definitely the closest thing this game gets to broken. The game has sidequests you can very often do, and while they're nothing super special, they're charming in their own right and I felt compelled to do them. The most fun (and realistic) aspect of the game is the fact that often times the main characters do not speak the native language of the country they are in, and thus cannot understand locals. This leads to both the characters AND the player sometimes having to interpret what is being said, which leads to some fun moments. And if you see a language you yourself know being represented, it adds to the fun of it, because you can actually understand the conversations you're not "supposed" to understand (German for me). Kinda feels like cheating, but in a good way. The only system that I did not understand was the morale system, since I didn't really notice the effects of it in my playthrough.

--------------------
The Average:

The characters are inoffensive: decent at best and boring at worst. Ivan was easily the best, standout character, playing the role of non-combatant very well in story, side quests and combat. He was definitely my favourite character. Rourke was kind of an emotional wreck all throughout the story, but mostly in an endearing way. His best aspects were his innocence and having to discover how to live as a "normal" human, while his idealism was his worst aspect from a writing perspective. Atiye and Pascal were fine additions, they had their funny and cute moments, don't have too much to say about them. Lynn's arc was incredibly predictable and while a lot of her backstory was resolved, some aspects still felt too vague. This unfortunately comes at the detriment of her character, because she isn't much without her backstory. The biggest disappointment was Adair, who unfortunately gets absolutely nothing to do in both the main story and the side content. Most often he just felt like a yes-man to Rourke. The side characters were fine. The villains were fine. The NPCs were fine. Most of the characters in this game were, unfortunately, just fine.

Unfortunately, the writing of the game was also very average. The story tackles serious topics like individuality, war, political gain, racism and actual human trafficking. For the most part, they really hit the nail on the head of the importance and effect of these topics on both the world in game and our real world. The problem is that the game has a very simple view of the conflicts and there's no room for nuance. There's an obvious "correct" answer to all of the conflicts that the game will throw in your face non-stop. I won't go into detail because I am not an expert on writing in general; I'm mostly saying this from a reader's perspective. The story is very predictable and simple. This is not necessarily a bad thing because we need some simplicity and happiness in our daily lives, especially in this day and age; I was just hoping for a bit more. The side content was very simple and unfortunately also suffers from being "in your face" about its messages. The best written parts of the story were the before-mentioned moments of Rourke and the gang just living life, especially the jazz scene and the scenes of Rourke hanging out with specific members of the group. Overall, I did enjoy the story, despite said predictability. I'd honestly love to read a story about the future of these characters, because despite my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about their simplicity, they did grow on me in the end.

--------------------
The Bad:

The main thing this game suffers from is bad controls and UI. I noticed that the game only uses about 6 total keys on the keyboard, 4 of which being the movement keys. Besides that, 1 button was used for pretty much everything in the game, while the last button was the "Back" button. The simplicity of the controls led to the game sometimes feeling like a slog to play, while also leading me to accidentally activate the menu over, and over, and over. In my head, I often made the comparison to the Zelda CDI games. While Long Gone Days is obviously not as bad as the CDI games, those games also suffered from having 1 button for many different action, despite more buttons being available to be implemented. The UI works at a base level, but it is very often unclear what certain parts do or which part of the menu has what information. Sometimes you get an item/weapon for one of the playable characters, but the game doesn't tell you who each item is for. That means you have to scour every single character's items in different parts of the menu to find what you just got. It's frankly just a tedious menu to navigate, both because of the controls and because of the UI.

The last thing I wanna mention is that the game speed is very, very slow. As far as I'm aware, there's no way to speed up dialogue boxes, which made reading go by pretty slow. The biggest offender of the slow game speed is the combat, specifically the buffs and debuffs. In the endgame, buffs are very important to stand a chance in the combat, and the strongest move in the game is a move that gives all of your party members +1 to each of their stats. The problem is that every single individual stat increase or decrease gets mentioned in its own dialogue box (which I just established goes by slowly), so using that move makes it so that you get 12 messages in a row telling you the characters' stats have increased. And then later when they go back down, the same thing happens. This section is the shortest section of my review, but trust me when I say that the game speed halted my fun of the game the most, because it often just felt like my time was being wasted.

--------------------
TL;DR

Art good, gameplay fun, characters and writing fine, controls and UI bad, game speed frustrating.

Long Gone Days — это игра, которая действительно оставила у меня яркие впечатления. Сразу хочется отметить, что графика в ней просто потрясающая. Пиксельный стиль, который использован, создает уникальную атмосферу, и я часто останавливался, чтобы просто полюбоваться окружающим миром. Каждая локация проработана с вниманием к деталям, и это добавляет игре особый шарм.

Сюжет меня тоже поразил. Он не просто о войне, а затрагивает глубокие темы, такие как предательство и поиск своего места в этом мире. Я реально переживал за главного героя и его выборы, ведь они влияют на развитие истории. Были моменты, когда я останавливался и задумывался о том, как бы я поступил на его месте. Это, на мой взгляд, огромный плюс — когда игра заставляет тебя задуматься.

Боевая система в игре тоже интересная. Она сочетает в себе элементы стратегии и экшена, что делает каждую битву уникальной. Я часто экспериментировал с разными подходами, подбирая персонажей в зависимости от ситуации. Это добавляет разнообразия в геймплей и заставляет думать, как лучше действовать.

Еще меня порадовало разнообразие персонажей. Каждый из них имеет свои уникальные способности, и это позволяет мне выбирать, как именно я хочу проходить игру. Иногда я даже возвращался назад, чтобы попробовать другой стиль боя с новым персонажем.

Не могу не упомянуть про звуковое оформление. Музыка и звуки отлично дополняют атмосферу игры. Бывают моменты, когда музыка усиливает напряжение или, наоборот, создает спокойное настроение, и это действительно помогает погрузиться в происходящее.

В целом, Long Gone Days — это игра, которая оставила у меня положительные эмоции. Она не просто развлекает, но и заставляет задуматься о важных вещах. Если вы любите истории с глубоким смыслом и интересный геймплей, обязательно дайте ей шанс!

[b]TLDR review:[/b]
[spoiler]Forgiving and recruiting a guy who murdered children and trafficked women is needed for the ‘good’ ending.[/spoiler] What did they mean by this?

[b]Longer review:[/b]
First, the good. The character design and overall art direction is great. The main cast is likeable. There's a foundation here that could have made a good story. That's more or less the only praise I have for this game.

I'll summarize using their listed features on the Steam page.

[b]A Nuanced Look at War: Experience the clash of modern conflict against civilian life through the contrast of intense RPG combat and slower, slice-of-life gameplay.[/b]

Nothing "nuanced" about it. This isn't Spec Ops: The Line, Come and See (1985), or the first few minutes of All Quiet on the Western Front (2022). This is Frodo and the Fellowship journeying to Mordor. This is the Pevensie siblings and the White Witch. This is the Avengers vs. Thanos.
There’s no “contrast” between intense and slice-of-life gameplay. The combat isn’t intense. It’s mind-numbing. Most of the brief moments of respite for the characters make no sense considering the urgency of the plot. For example, [spoiler]Lynn decides to sit down with Atiye to discuss her past trauma in the middle of them escaping capture and trying to rescue Adair and Rourke who are getting dragged into a train going who knows where.[/spoiler]

[b]Communication is Key: As Long Gone Days is set in the real world, you'll encounter several language barriers. Recruit interpreters in order to communicate with others and forge bonds beyond borders.[/b]

Not worth listing as a feature. The interpreters are just the main cast and you meet them almost immediately the moment they're needed. 
Cool concept to acknowledge the language barrier though.

[b]Strength in Others: Meet a colorful cast of potential comrades. Grow relationships through your words and actions as you live and fight together.[/b]

Only as far as their design and the tropes they fill. Within the actual story, they’re all one dimensional and didn’t develop in any meaningful way.
Minor spoilers for the main characters.

- Rourke and Adair [spoiler]break 20 years of brainwashing the moment it’s challenged.[/spoiler]
- Vanya [spoiler]is a conscientious objector but promises to do what’s necessary. This is never challenged.[/spoiler]
- Lynn [spoiler]has trauma from being kidnapped by human traffickers. She reveals and overcomes it all in the same level.[/spoiler]
- Atiye [spoiler]feels bad about not helping her friend investigate a bunch of fascists, so she picks up a gun.[/spoiler]
- Pascal [spoiler]feels bad about helping the human traffickers, so he picks up a gun.[/spoiler]

[b]Keep Morale High: Choose dialogue options wisely to boost morale in battle. Every character has distinct personality traits and motivations.[/b]

The morale system is bad design. It’s one of two factors for the ending and it makes no sense for both the narrative and the gameplay.
As an example, if you have low morale, you are locked out of a quest to [spoiler]help Vanya's neighbor find her missing daughter. Vanya will ask Rourke for permission (for some reason) and Rourke will refuse saying we don't have time.[/spoiler]But you know what is available despite the low morale? [spoiler]A little further down the road, we can help a random stranger with finding every stray dog and cat in the area.[/spoiler]

[b]Strategic RPG Combat: Spot and take down targets from afar in Sniper Mode, or engage up-close in front-view, turn-based combat. Target specific parts of an enemy’s body for a tactical advantage.[/b]

You have iirc 3 times where you enter “sniper mode”. It’s not your choice, it happens at specific points. There is one where you get the option [spoiler]which results in a morale loss because Rourke feels bad about killing these armed nazis (who kidnapped Zoe) in particular and not the rest.[/spoiler] You click to snipe and there’s a timer that resets when it runs out.
The “up-close combat” is engaging in the same way that a cangue keeps a prisoner awake by jabbing into their neck. It requires enough attention that you can’t just mash the attack button, but doesn’t compensate in any way to make it enjoyable.

[b]No Random Encounters: Every battle is hand-crafted and directly related to the plot. Your choices in battle will shape your party's lives, and the world around them.[/b]

No random encounters is great, but the 10 or so unique non-boss enemies you encounter over and over are all functionally the same. Either regular attacks or regular attacks + heals.
You get some dialogue choices during boss fights (there’s 5), but they don’t affect anything save for one near the end which is the 2nd factor for the ending.
Specific dialogue choices do reward morale, but it’s ridiculous because the options hardly feel any different.
Example 1:
[spoiler]"Because they taught me to see the world in a new light."[/spoiler]
[spoiler]"Because they have done the same for me."[/spoiler]
Example 2:
[spoiler]"They make me strong."[/spoiler]
[spoiler]"They don't need my power. They have their own.”[/spoiler]
Which choices do you think give morale and which don’t?

[b]Ending (major spoilers)[/b]
A single playthrough takes about 12-15 hours and I did both endings.
In the “good” ending, you beat the big bad and our characters return to their lives because you kept a positive attitude and chose to see the light in Coyle’s baby killing, human trafficking eyes. 
In the “bad” ending, your characters will have to spend probably the rest of their lives as fugitives because you weren’t optimistic enough and failed to recruit the war criminal. Note that our characters WANT to recruit him. You only affect it by succeeding or failing.

Some of my problems listed:
- Our characters don’t immediately subdue Father General, who might as well be mustache man. I get that this is supposed to be a thematic face-off of ideas but this allows—
- Mustache man to send an order to shoot protesters outside. An action that will ruin decades of propaganda work, just to prove a point that “people cannot govern themselves” and will “turn into animals trying to escape death”.
- Neither of the two endings cover what happens in the rest of the world. We’re only told what our main characters are personally up to.
- Why is morale a factor for the ending when our characters take the exact same actions regardless? What narrative purpose does morale play aside from locking you out of side quests?
- Why does the “good” ending require clemency for an organization that killed children and kidnapped women to “sustain” their army to then be disposed of when they no longer can?
- Spontaneous movements happen, but organizing a protest of thousands in one night using just a projector to display some powerpoint slides onto a building goes beyond even the most spontaneous of movements.

Look. If you asked me whether I enjoyed playing this, my answer would be a yes despite my disappointment. All the ingredients for something great are there, but the story is an absolute nothingburger that wastes all that potential. It fails to convey anything but general platitudes (that are arguably harmful) that aren’t even consistently displayed through the characters’ actions. 

All of the issues we see in the game? False flag terrorism, refugee crises, human trafficking, crypto-fascists? These are just a backdrop for what is a run of the mill JRPG story where a group of plucky young people seek to defeat god (or a god-like figure in this case). You're not fighting a global system. You're fighting the boogieman. What message does it convey about the real world where these things are very real and very relevant?

Also there's an achievement to NOT pet the dog. What did they mean by this?

Pros;

- For a game with the "Choices Matter" tag, choice really does not matter at all in this game. You may get a single line of dialogue change but no new information or different outcome is possible which really undercuts whenever you can make a choice.
- Combat has a lot of ludo-narrative dissonance. You play as a sniper yet there are few sniping sections and combat tends to be a direct head on event at point blank range.
- How to save is poorly explained and it is far too easy to accidentally close the game without saving

Summary;
The lore gives the story a lot of potential it does almost nothing with in a game that feels like a direct to streaming TV show that is getting cancelled after one season. It sounds harsh, but this game barely delivers on the basics listed on the store page.

[h1]Análise de [b]Long Gone Days[/b][/h1]

[h2][b]Resumo Geral[/b][/h2]
*Long Gone Days* é um RPG de turnos indie que se destaca pela sua narrativa imersiva e visual pixel art encantador. A história aborda temas maduros, como política, moralidade e escolhas pessoais, envolvendo o jogador em um enredo profundo e impactante. Com personagens bem desenvolvidos e mecânicas únicas, é uma experiência que cativa e deixa uma marca significativa.

---

[h2][b]Pontos Positivos[/b][/h2]

[b]1. Narrativa e Personagens:[/b]
A trama do jogo é um dos seus pontos mais fortes. Focando em uma conspiração política de uma organização poderosa, o protagonista decide ir contra tudo o que aprendeu desde pequeno, o que gera conflitos emocionais e decisões difíceis. O enredo é cativante e surpreende com um final inesperado, trazendo um realismo raro ao gênero. Os personagens são profundamente desenvolvidos e cativantes, com arcos de evolução que os tornam memoráveis.

[b]2. Estilo Visual e Atmosfera:[/b] 
A pixel art é apaixonante e combina perfeitamente com a proposta do jogo, trazendo um charme único que reforça a imersão. Apesar de ser simples, o estilo visual é marcante e bem executado.

[b]3. Jogabilidade:[/b]
A jogabilidade de turnos é intuitiva e funciona bem para o gênero. A adição de mecânicas únicas, como a escolha de partes específicas do corpo para atacar, traz uma camada estratégica interessante. Os puzzles, embora não muito desafiadores, são divertidos e ajudam a variar o ritmo.

[b]4. Momentos Memoráveis:[/b]
O jogo oferece cenas tocantes e significativas, como o momento de tocar jazz com o grupo ou assistir desenhos animados, que destacam a humanidade dos personagens. Esses momentos aumentam a conexão emocional do jogador com a história.

[b]5. Preço Acessível:[/b]
Para um jogo indie, o preço é justo e oferece um excelente custo-benefício, considerando a qualidade da narrativa e o visual impecável.

---

[h2][b]Pontos a Melhorar[/b][/h2]

[b]1. Trilha Sonora:[/b] 
Embora a trilha sonora seja boa, há momentos em que ela parece inadequada ao clima, como músicas tranquilas em situações tensas. Um ajuste nesse aspecto poderia aumentar ainda mais a imersão.

[b]2. Progressão:[/b]
A ausência de um sistema de level up pode não agradar a todos os jogadores. O sistema de equipamentos é funcional, mas não entrega a sensação de progressão recompensadora que muitos RPGs proporcionam.

[b]3. Rejogabilidade Limitada:[/b]
Apesar de haver finais alternativos e missões extras, a experiência pode não atrair jogadores que buscam grande variedade ou mudanças significativas na história principal.

---

[h2][b]Conclusão[/b][/h2]
*Long Gone Days* é um jogo que brilha em sua narrativa madura, personagens bem construídos e visual deslumbrante.

[h2][b]Recomendação:[/b][/h2]
Para quem busca um RPG com história envolvente, personagens inesquecíveis e um toque de estratégia, este jogo é altamente recomendado. Seu preço acessível é apenas mais um motivo para não deixar esta obra-prima indie passar despercebida.  

[b]Nota Final:[/b] 9/10

RPGzinho bem bacana sobre geopolítica ambientado em lugares reais como Polônia, Alemanha e Rússia. Aborda um grupo paramilitar que se infiltra nos governos para promover conflitos de acordo com seus interesses. Você joga com um sniper desse grupo e outros personagens se juntam a você. O combate é por turnos, como em RPGs clássicos, realizado com armas de fogo (aqui todo mundo resiste a vários tiros, né?).  A trama é muito boa, os gráficos são ao estilo 16 bits e as cutscenes e os diálogos são em estilo anime (o que caiu muito bem no jogo). Não existe nível, então não há preocupação com "grind". Aliás, o jogo é muito fácil (eu mesmo não perdi em nenhum chefe). Parece que o jogo está mais preocupado com o fato de você desfrutar da história, poder acompanhar o desenrolar dos eventos sem ficar preso por questões de evolução de força de personagens. A única coisa que poderiam ter explorado mais é o modo sniper do jogo, que só ocorre em apenas três momentos durante toda a campanha e foi um dos grandes motivos que me fizeram decidir adquirir o game. Mas isso não tira em nada a graça e o brilho de Long Gone Days. Recomendo.

[h2]剧本还行，玩法酷刑[/h2]

我其实觉得，作为一部反战反独裁作品，本作还是做得挺不错的；至少，主次要角色的特点还是比较鲜明的——从犹豫踌躇到意志坚定的叛兵、信仰公正又有所隐忍的记者、技术上灵活斡旋而人际上言辞笨拙的极客、自我洗脑因而荒唐可笑的独裁者及其走狗，等等。音乐挺不错、立绘也挺养眼的。

奈何最终还是在二元的“好评还是差评”中选择了差评，是因为玩了11小时通关主线以后，才发现主线内容其实只能撑得起4-5个小时，剩下的时间全部浪费在了无味的战斗、跑腿、手动存档和解谜中。因为地图不大，引导弱也不算一个太大的问题；然而记不住地图往往是跑图过程中极为痛苦的一件事情。有的时候地图里实在没地方放东西的时候，会整一个推箱子、按按钮什么的解谜要素来硬凑跑图时间。有时角色之间的对话会极其注水，而且你必须等待这句话全部显示完毕才能浏览下一句话。

然而，跟“战斗”比起来，痛苦万分的跑图和索然无味的支线简直就是小巫见大巫。整个游戏打完，我甚至还搞不清楚“防御力(DEF)”和“敏捷度(AGI)”究竟对减伤和闪避有何影响，更别提“运气(LUK)”了。在自己的回合中，任意一次攻击的闪避概率都是看不到的——有些敌人即便攻击头部也不会躲闪，然而另一些敌人即便攻击身体也有~50%的闪避概率。而且回合制战斗本身还有一个缺点：战斗关卡一变多就会很烦人——跑图拿某某道具的时候，有时不得不应战，然后这场战斗会硬拖你至少五分钟的游戏时间。

于是乎，一场较为困难的战斗变成了这样子：我方第一回合先给自己上群体buff、给敌方上群体debuff，敌方第一回合给自己上群体buff。每一次行动中，每有一个受到影响的单位，右上角的UI上都会显示“某某的攻击力获得增益！”（是的，每三个回合，当我上一个“为所有队友提供攻击力、防御力和敏捷度增益”的buff时，UI上会有12条记录闪过，而且还无法跳过！！）。敌我一套buff上完，虽然游戏里才过去了一个回合，但是电脑前已经过去了近五分钟了。在boss战中，敌我双方起码要上三四轮buff互相消耗——虽然我承认我比较菜、打法比较保守，但是一场boss战我平均打了大约半个小时。更折磨的是，战斗的本身难度其实很低，打完一场boss战一点点成就感都没有。本来大约五分钟能解决的一场精英/boss战，被这个拉跨的UI拖得太久了。

And then... the combat. Oh the combat.

The combat, which is so so slow. It barely has any depth and instead it makes you feel like you need to play carefully early on but that's because you do nothing but exchange regular attacks back-and-forth. But what about the fact that you can hit different body parts?! Doesn't matter, just aim for the head. High evasion just means a give or take 5% chance to miss whilst the damage boost is around 20% higher than the body. But what about the arm, it has a chance to paralyse? Don't bother, you can try to fish for it, but then you'll keep taking damage instead of just finishing the fight asap. Stat boosts are nice, but last only three turns and the text is slooooooow. Props to Atiye, who can't even try to hit for the head and as such, despite having a massive shotgun, doesn't deal that much damage and becomes the least useful party member, shame really.

But you get all these nifty abilities! Yeah and it doesn't matter because they deal less damage overall; have a small animation which means combat takes longer; they cost SP, which never recovers itself outside of a single time and even iif there is a secondary effect, it is a very small chance! Notable exceptions are Ivan's team-wide boosts, Aidar's healing and Pascals high-chance to paralyse attack. Speaking of paralyse. You're facing a tough boss? Then just use paralysis as it is king. Just don't bother with any other status conddition because it removes paralysis! Blind is just fishing for luck when you could also just do damage and bleed is barely a thing to begin with.

Then they offer you this really tough choice between stat-boosting equipment or a healing item on one side or recovering SP on the other. But that doesn't matter, because you'll barely use SP at all.

Puzzles are barely puzzles as well, which is fine I guess, but if the combat is a slog and the puzzles aren't really up to snuff, what am I doing aside trying to enjoy the story? Which I did, sometimes, kinda, by the way, but not enough to justify the amount of time it took. Creating a vicious loop of disappointment.

Oh also, spoiler-warning from now on. I guess.

SPOILERS

The fake out at the beginning as a tutorial. Man was I disappointed. I really looked forward to getting to find out how we got to that point where there's seemingly impossible odds, stuck at the frontline in a strange land. Only for it to be far more mundane that it actually was.

Why am I being punished with only getting the bad ending when I gave mister 'I can change sides' all the time in the world when he was at low health to initiate the required dialogue?! I spend 10 rounds just spamming useless recovery items to try and get him to talk, but to no avail. Was it because I paralysed him repeatedly until he got to low health? I'll never know. But at that point I just gave up, finished him and finished the game. Admittedly, I do enjoy the way the bad ending is framed: there's no guarantee that beheading an organisation means the organisation just kinda, ends. But again, it is the end of game, there's nothing more to it.

I don't know, I just wish they focused more on the fish-out-of-water idea, the foundation was there. Instead our main protaganist just kinda.... pouts and whines a bit sometimes. Other times he just flat out says he doesn't understand something and it's cleared up immediately or he somehow knows things he really shouldn't considering he's a CHILD SOLDIER.

SPOILERS END

All in all, interesting concepts; wasted opportunities.

I think the worst part is that I saw the potential, I really wished it had reached some of it at least, but now I just feel kinda... disappointed.
